entries.title: Retrospec Joe Rev 2 Review (2026): Putting the ‘Joy’ in Joyride
entries.summary: This affordable electric BMX delighted my entire family, even if its range, ride comfort, and actual BMX abilities are limited.
entries.content:
Fun, retro style that appeals to both teens and adults. Well-priced. UL-2271 and 2849 certified. Frame triangle is big enough to attach a folding lock.

TIRED

Seat is cheap-feeling and very hard. No suspension and no way to carry cargo. Range takes a huge hit on hills. No battery IP rating for water resistance. Not a “real” BMX.

Though I’ve since gotten used to it, every time I ride the electric blue Joe Rev 2 electric BMX, people stare. Their heads turn as they drive past, eyes narrowed. “Is that an adult riding a BMX bike?” I imagine the thought process going. “Why is it so fast? Why is it so big?” These are valid questions, and they all have the same answer: Because it’s fun.

In fact, my entire family has taken turns riding this bike all over town for the past four weeks, testing it up and down hills, taking it on grocery runs, and even staying out riding until the battery drained. The verdict? The Joe Rev 2 may not be the smoothest ride, but for the price, it’s a unique and worthwhile option for basic cruising and casual riding.

All Eyes on Me

California-based Retrospec specializes in affordable outdoor toys; primarily paddleboards, longboards, bikes, and no-frills ebikes like the foldable Judd Rev 2, which WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani wrote “captures the vibe of being a 12-year-old kid and riding your bike more than anything I’ve ridden in some time.”

The entry-level Joe Rev was created in this same spirit—a full-sized, BMX-inspired frame with fun color options (electric blue, matte gray), 3-inch tan wall balloon tires, and those unmistakable handlebars. There are no apps or fancy readouts, no lights, and no shocks. Just five levels of pedal assist and a throttle attached to a single-speed drivetrain and 750-watt rear-hub motor.

“No cream, no sugar” is even printed on the chain stays, lest one forget the minimalist doctrine. On the plus side, this lack of bones allows the Joe Rev 2 to weigh in on the lighter side at 56 pounds.

This is the second iteration of the original Joe Rev, which is still available (for now) at the sale price of $1,200. The Rev 2 sports a bigger 500 Wh battery with a listed 60-mile range (up from 48 miles) and an updated display. Namely, a 2-by-2.5-inch LCD screen on the left handlebar displaying power level, battery life, and speed, as opposed to the original’s bare-basic hub with buttons.

The battery can be quickly locked and unlocked from the bottom of the frame with a key and charges from red to full green in several hours; it weighs about 7 pounds, so it’s easy enough to carry in a backpack, though at 18 inches long, it could be a tight fit if your bag is already packed.

Teen Spirit

At one point during the testing period, my almost-14-year-old son, who is 5’ 10” and 145 pounds, took the Joe Rev 2 out on a full battery to see how long he could ride in our town of hills. We were all surprised to find he hit the red “recharge” light in about 20 miles. It shouldn't have been too much of a shock, given that the hills were steep, and he was using the throttle primarily. But it is a good reminder that, like all ebikes, the Joe Rev 2’s range will vary dramatically depending on rider weight, speed, and conditions.

Interestingly, there’s an ominous warning sticker on the Joe Rev’s frame that states no one under 16 is to ride this bike. It does have pedals and a maximum speed of 20 mph, making it a Class 2 ebike—legal in many, if not, most states for kids under 16.

When I asked Retrospec if there was anything specific about the Joe Rev 2 that would preclude younger teens from riding it, their rep told me the company “follows the most stringent regulations across the markets where their ebikes are sold. As a result, their minimum recommended rider age is 16. If local laws permit younger riders, such as a 12-year-old, it is ultimately up to parents or guardians to determine whether their child has the maturity, experience, and ability to safely operate an ebike.”

However, an adult-sized, mature 14- or 15-year-old could be a gray area. My son is allowed to ride the Joe Rev 2 occasionally, but not regularly. If you decide to go this route, know this bike was deemed acceptable by several teens in my orbit, though stylistically a couple notches below the e-moto-style frames popularized by brands like MacFox.

How It Rides

As is typical with ebikes, some assembly of the Joe Rev 2 is required upon arrival. Chiefly, attaching the wheels, pedals, and handlebars, for which it comes with a generously sized set of hex wrenches. The first night, it took a couple of tries to get the front wheel seated properly—there was a slight wobble during my husband’s inaugural ride around the block, but after further tightening, it has not resurfaced. The brakes are mechanical disc with 180 mm rotors, which also occasionally needed tightening, but otherwise caused no issues during the testing period.

My own first ride was on a flat surface, around the parking lot of my son’s former elementary school. I found that the five levels of pedal assist kick in quickly and almost forcefully; the throttle is an easy-to-use thumb switch located on the left handlebar. The frame feels like a good size for my height (5’ 6”), and the whole setup was easy to parse in just a couple of minutes.

Aside from the lack of suspension—you will feel every bump—my only major complaint is the seat. In fact, my butt still hurts as I write this from even a short ride yesterday. The Joe Rev 2's seat is hard, plasticky, and small—definitely worth swapping out if you’re going to be commuting on this or otherwise riding it daily.

My 5’ 8” husband rides the Joe Rev 2 to the grocery store several times a week, an activity he greatly enjoys, and over time we’ve found ourselves wishing there were an easy way to carry cargo, such as the ability to bolt on a basket or saddlebags. To be fair, though, I’m not sure it would ultimately be worth the reduction in range, though the bike does have a payload capacity of 350 pounds. We do, however, greatly appreciate the open space in the frame to attach a folding lock. (We went with the Seatlylock FoldyLock for $90).

One thing I have not yet been able to test is the water resistance. I live in western Washington state, where it rains nine months out of the year, and the Joe Rev 2's battery is mounted at the bottom of the down tube, where it could easily be splashed. There's no given IP rating for water resistance, so while I'm sure the battery housing can handle a light, occasional spray, riding the bike on a super-rainy day would make me nervous.

It also bears mentioning that if you're hoping for a real BMX bike with which you can do tricks, the Joe Rev 2 is not that. Insofar as being a BMX, the only quality seems to be the handlebars. Nothing about it feels nimble, and at this weight, you’re not taking it to the skate park—the only jumps and rail hops happening are in your imagination.

However, if you do happen to lose control of yourself and break something, the Joe Rev 2 is UL 2849 Certified for the electrical system and UL 2271 Certified for the battery, meaning that, unlike with many other internet-purchased direct-to-consumer bikes, your local bike shop may be able to repair it. Though this depends heavily on the type of repair needed; it’s worth calling to be sure.

Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech. As a forestry major at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Kat practiced axe throwing on her college logging team and trained as a wildland firefighter ... Read More

entries.title: This Beautifully Weird Necklace Is Secretly a USB Drive
entries.summary: Noware’s Puff necklace whimsically reimagines flash drives, turning something functional into personalized jewelry.
entries.content:
I’m already growing hoarse in Golden Gate Park as Charli XCX takes the stage at a San Francisco music festival. The crowd starts jumping as a guitar hook hits, and I reluctantly comply, bouncing around on these aging knees as my chunky Puff necklace almost flies off the chain.

During a lull in the set, someone next to me compliments the necklace, which has stainless steel swirls and a bulbous orange center. Their eyes grow wide as I flip the cap off and explain that it’s a hidden USB flash drive—I plugged the Puff into my phone to show off the animations.

When Harry Isaac and Sebastian Bidegain, working together under the Noware moniker, posted an early prototype of their retro-futuristic necklace on social media in 2025, it quickly racked up over a million views with thousands of waitlist sign-ups to buy one. The duo has spent the last year attempting to turn the online attention on their prototype into a mass-produced reality. Now, Noware is finally ready to ship units this October.

The pair arrived at the WIRED office wearing Puff necklaces, naturally, that match with their trendy gorpcore outfits. They seem nervous, albeit excited, to show off their creation. Neither has had a wide release for their products before, though both are well-versed in whimsical designs. Isaac previously went viral for making an electric scooter that shoots out bubbles. Bidegain was already sculpturally approaching electronics, with prototypes like a vape camera and lo-fi sampler built into a rock.

The design ethos of the Puff is just as much about aesthetics as it is about usefulness. Noware’s marketing materials show a cool girl with a Puff clipped onto her purse, where a Labubu might have sat last year, as well as styled on her neck with a pile of other silver chains. Bidegain says the “squishy, doughy” textures of food partially inspired Puff’s design, as well as cellular biology and tactile devices, like old phones and radios.

“On one end, I want anyone to be able to wear it, just if they think it's pretty,” he says. “Though, I also want people who actually find utility in flash drives as part of their workflow: photographers, DJs, IT people.”

The small screen in the middle of the necklace is my favorite aspect. When it’s plugged into my phone or laptop, Puff’s center lights up with a customizable design. The Noware duo showed me goopy animations that reacted to the direction I held the phone as well as an aquarium mode. They even put the WIRED logo on it through custom software anyone can use to craft their own designs. The Puff doesn’t have an internal battery, so the USB drive can live as a piece of jewelry far longer than the expiration date of most electronics.

The necklace’s biggest drawback is its price: a whopping $179 for only 128 GB of storage. A basic flash drive with similar storage costs around $30. The duo doesn’t want the Puff to remain that expensive and hopes to reach a more accessible price. “We want it to get cheaper over time, but we're just trying to make it exist first,” says Isaac. They blame it partially on the inflated cost of memory right now, thanks to the AI boom. Depending on how Puff’s initial release goes, future iterations may include more budget-friendly options, like a nonmetal version.

This experimental device from two New York City-based makers was the perfect accessory for a weekend-long festival, with its retro-futuristic vibe and sharp colors.

“We're very interested in making electronics that are more opinionated, playful, and personal,” Isaac says. It was a lighthearted conversation piece as I made small talk with vendors, and at least one friend assumed I was hiding drugs in it. (Nope, just a bunch of nudes.)

entries.title: 6 Best Apple Watch Accessories to Upgrade Your Watch (2026)
entries.summary: These are the Apple Watch accessories I recommend adding to your setup.
entries.content:
If you have an iPhone, you've probably considered buying an Apple Watch—and with good reason. It's the best smartwatch and best fitness tracker for iPhone owners, and it allows you to make calls, send texts, pay for purchases, and more without reaching for your phone. That said, I’m a firm believer that your Apple Watch is only as good as the accessories that support it.

The right band can make it comfortable enough to wear all day and night for sleep tracking. A charging stand will remind you to keep it topped up, and a protective case could save you from a shattered screen. To help upgrade your Apple Watch setup, I, along with a few of my WIRED colleagues, tested chargers, bands, cases, and more to find the accessories worth the money. I’d also recommend getting AppleCare, which is the company's extended warranty plan, given that service pricing for watch repairs is exorbitant.

For more smart accessories, check out our guides to the Best Apple 3-in-1 Chargers and Best Apple Watch Bands.

Featured in This Guide

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Apple Watch Band

When you buy your Apple Watch, you get to choose a band at checkout. I find textile and metal (stainless steel or titanium) bands to be more comfortable and fashionable than fluoroelastomer bands, which tend to be rigid and can irritate your skin. I love the Nike Sport Loop so much that it's been my everyday band for six years, and I ended up buying it in two colors: navy blue and black. Made from recycled polyester, Spandex, and nylon, it's soft, breathable, and easy to hand-wash. The Velcro pull tab makes it as adjustable as a band can get, and it's easy to fasten with one hand. Apple doesn't advertise any water resistance, but I've swum with it multiple times; after rinsing it off and letting it air dry, it looked brand new. The yarn is reflective if you're running at night, though it is subtle.

The band comes in five colors and three case sizes, which makes it compatible with most versions of the Apple Watch. If you're shopping for a leather band, Konsu NYC makes a gorgeous strap, too. For more recommendations, check out our Best Apple Watch Bands guide.

Best Charging Stand

The Nomad Stand One Max is a splurge, costing even more than reviewer Simon Hill’s top pick (the Belkin 3-in-1 Qi2 Charging Stand), but its minimalist design is arguably worth the extra spend. It’s compact enough that it doesn’t overcrowd a nightstand, and with the cable tucked away, it looks sleek. It’s also one of our favorites for fast Apple Watch charging, along with Qi2 25-watt charging for iPhones and MagSafe devices. The angled charging pad supports your phone in either portrait or landscape orientation, and the Apple Watch puck allows for Nightstand mode. It comes in three colors and includes a durable, braided 6.6-foot USB-C cable. The only downside is that there’s no included power adapter. Nomad’s 40W Slim Power Adapter ($25) is an easy add-on, but it does increase the cost of an already pricey charger.

Best Portable Charger

A fully charged Apple Watch should last all day, but since I don't always remember to top it up, I always carry a power bank for backup when I'm out. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill—who specializes in smartphone accessories—says the compact Anker MagGo Power Bank is the best portable Apple Watch charger. It can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It has a 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and its built-in USB-C cable and USB-C port offer up to 30 watts to your phone or small device. Plus, it comes in white, black, teal, and pink for whimsy.

Best Apple Watch Case

Unlike a phone, a watch is worn on your wrist, so every millimeter of real estate counts. If all you want is a thin, affordable, and attractive bumper that will protect your watch from bangs and scratches throughout the day, this is my favorite. It's made from a matte thermoplastic urethane (TPU) that is extremely thin and fits a 41-mm watch well. I have and like the dark green color, but reviewers say the lighter colors show dirt very easily, so I would stick with darker shades.

Runner-Up: The Spigen Thin Fit ($15) is also a very nice, minimal case. But it's a bit pricier, and the plastic is not as soft to the touch. —Adrienne So

Best Apple Watch Screen Protector

Like bands, the best screen protector is not always the most expensive one. I tried pricier options from Spigen and Zagg, but when I pushed or pulled a case on over them, the thin films peeled off or bubbled. This screen protector (also made from TPU) was easy to apply and looks invisible once it's on. I particularly like the small rubber installation pad, which held the watch much more securely than other installation plates.

Even if it's reasonably easy to use, I recommend watching the short instructional video before putting it on your watch. Don't worry—if you mess up, it comes with several replacements. —Adrienne So

Best Storage for Apple Watch Bands

Even the most restrained and minimalist among us probably have at least two bands: a nylon sport loop for everyday wear, and a titanium or steel band for dressing up. You could always keep your spare bands in a shoebox on your dresser, but I like this hanger from Twelve South. The wall mount is incredibly easy to install; the bands slot neatly in a compressive groove at the top. Each holder fits up to six bands, but you can easily add more if your collection is bigger than mine. —Adrienne So

More Accessories WIRED Likes

Nomad Universal Cable for Apple Watch for $89: As WIRED reviewer Simon Hill notes in his Best USB-C Cables guide, this Nomad cable is overpriced. However, it’s undeniably handy because it can charge both your iPhone and Apple Watch. It's Kevlar-reinforced, and the braided finish is nice. You can also charge your AirPods on the charging puck as well as your watch. —Adrienne So

Belkin 3-in-1 Qi2 Charging Stand for $90: Even though Apple markedly improved the battery life on the Apple Watch in 2025, it still won't last for longer than 24 hours on a single charge. If you have an iPhone, AirPods, and an Apple Watch, a 3-in-1 charging station keeps everything organized, reduces cable clutter, and ensures your devices are always ready to go. Reviewer Simon Hill says the Belkin 3-in-1 Qi2 Charging Stand is the best money can buy. Thanks to its Qi2 certification, it can fast-charge an Apple Watch Ultra and Series 7 or newer, but it's also compatible with all other Apple Watches. Hill appreciates the chrome aesthetic of this particular stand; its treelike structure suspends two gadgets in midair (MagSafe-compatible), with a spot for an AirPods case on the circular band.

Insta360 X5 360 Camera for $550: Overlay your fitness stats over your video while filming with the Insta360 X series. Simply connect the camera to the Insta360 app and authorize it to connect to Apple Health. The Insta360 X5 also connects to Garmin and GPS devices. Great for any vlogger showing the world their fitness journey. —Adrienne So

Avoid These Accessories

Zagg InvisibleShield GlassFusion Screen Protector for $30: There is no earthly reason why this screen protector should be so expensive. It also bubbled within several days. —Adrienne So

What Am I Testing Next?

I’m testing the Anker Prime Wireless Charging Station and retesting the Anker MagGo Power Bank.

entries.title: Instapaper, the Original Read-It-Later App, Just Got a Huge Upgrade
entries.summary: New fonts, better customization, and a whole new layout all make it worth dusting off your Instapaper account.
entries.content:
As you've no doubt noticed, there's a lot to read on the internet. Vast numbers of new articles are published every day. There's still quite a lot of it not being written by AI, too.

Trying to keep up with everything can feel exhausting, and that's where read-it-later apps come in. These apps will queue up content that catches your eye as you go to and fro across the web, and keep these articles, videos, blog posts, and social media updates bookmarked until you get a chance to catch up with them. When it’s time to dig in, the apps present the articles in a clean, uncluttered layout.

It's a neat idea, but it needs to be well implemented for it to work—otherwise you can spend more time compiling and organizing your reading than actually catching up on your queue.

Instapaper is one of the oldest read-it-later apps, having launched back in 2008. It's also still one of the best options, even more so now that it's been given a major revamp. Here's what's new, and why it might be worth your while diving back into your Instapaper account (or signing up for the first time).

Instapaper Basics

Instapaper is available for the web, Android, and iOS, and reflows web articles into a tidily arranged, distraction-free format that doesn't feature any ads, menus, or other onscreen furniture. You just get the text and the images, so reading the articles you've saved is a more pleasurable experience than it is on the web.

You can customize the Instapaper interface in a variety of ways. The apps let you change the font style, size, and spacing, and adjust the background color of the “paper” that the text and images are placed on.

Everything is neatly arranged on the screen, too. You get estimates for how long each article will take to read (as well as the option to see summaries of the text). You can use folders and tags to categorize saved posts in a variety of ways. Also, everything syncs seamlessly across all the devices you're using Instapaper on.

Getting articles into Instapaper—a crucial part of the process—is straightforward. On mobile you can pass web links into the app through the standard share tools, while on desktop you can either paste the URLs straight into Instapaper, or use the extensions that are available for the most popular browsers.

You can add and store an unlimited number of articles in Instapaper for free. There's also a premium package available for $6 a month or $60 a year, which removes the ads from the apps, and gives you extras like a search tool, Kindle support, and the option to have your saved articles read out to you.

Instapaper's Big 2026 Update

I've been using Instapaper very happily for years, but not so much recently. That's nothing to do with Instapaper, really. It's more about an increase in work and family commitments, and having less time than I'd like just to read. It also means that my read-it-later list has grown to a scary length.

Now the service has got its biggest update in quite some time, which means I've got a good excuse to log back in and start chipping away at all the articles I've been meaning to read. The web app revamp is actually only the second full rewrite of the Instapaper code since the service launched, and it brings with it an elegant three-column layout that keeps everything in view and works really well on wide displays (like mine).

Other improvements include keyboard shortcuts (which I noticed are shown on screen next to menus when you start clicking around), and a new multi-select feature. You can now select all of the articles in a specific list, as well as using Shift+Click to select a range of articles in the queue.

Over on iOS, the app has been given a full Liquid Glass refresh, and there are several improvements that cover section counts, section sorting, and a wider choice of appearance options (including new fonts). The existing AI Voices feature, which reads out articles in the synthetic AI voice of your choosing, has now made its way to Android, too.

If you're a premium Instapaper user, you can have articles read out by tapping the three dots up in the top right corner when a saved item is open. This can come in handy when you can't read articles but can listen to them—when you're driving or walking, or tackling the endless list of chores that need doing at home.

entries.title: Auk Mini 2 Indoor Smart Garden Review: Better Where It Counts
entries.summary: Auk’s Mini 2 improves on the original model with better lights, a sleeker design, and fun new colors.
entries.content:
When Auk’s original Mini 1 herb garden hit the market in 2024, it touched on something that many tabletop gardens had until that point failed to consider: If you’re going to give up that much counter or table space, you don’t want it to be for something ugly.

Aerogardens and similar models look … fine, but you’re probably not going to see one in the background of an Architectural Digest shoot. The Auk Mini filled that marketplace gap with its pairing of sleek Scandinavian design and utility, transforming the run-of-the-mill herb-growing operation into a conversation piece.

When I reviewed the original Auk Mini last fall, I loved that it allowed users to plant their own seeds in widely available coco coir, an alternative to peat moss made from coconut husks. No proprietary pods, no subscriptions, no fussy app.

When I started testing the brand-new Auk 2 earlier this summer, I wondered what new features could possibly justify a new model. Turns out, there was more room for improvement than I thought.

Same but Different

For the uninitiated, Auk (pronounced “owk”) is a Norwegian company that released its first garden, the Auk 1, in 2021. Essentially a larger version of the Mini 1, the Auk 1 received mixed reviews online for its tower water reservoir and inconsistent light and watering cycles. (In fact, a former WIRED director tested it and became so frustrated that he threw it in the trash.)

entries.title: Zyzz Was the Original Looksmaxxer. His Rise and Untimely Death Feel More Relevant Than Ever
entries.summary: A new Apple documentary explores the life of Aziz “Zyzz” Shavershian, who rocketed to internet fame in an age before influencers, then died at age 22 in 2011.
entries.content:
“We’re all gonna make it, brah!”

That was the aspirational rallying cry of Aziz Shavershian, better known by his online alias, Zyzz. Once the shy and skinny son of Kurdish parents who struggled to find his place in Sydney, Australia, where the family had moved from Russia, he’d thrown himself wholeheartedly into fitness, spending hours at the gym every day and frequenting the infamous Bodybuilding.com and 4chan forums.

In time, the teenager’s chiseled physique gave him the confidence to develop an online persona that had little in common with the gentle and goofy kid that his friends and family knew. This would be Zyzz, a brash raver who strutted, mugged, danced, and flexed shirtless in front of his webcam while asking if viewers were “mirin’” (that is, admiring his body) and exhorting other men to chase their self-improvement goals. By 2010, his videos had made him an Australian celebrity with fans around the globe.

And as of August 2011, he was dead in Thailand, at the age of 22.

Shavershian’s brief and tragic life is the basis of a new documentary, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz, now available on Apple TV and Prime Video. But this keenly nuanced film is more than the familiar tale of an ambitious youth who pursued fame at all costs. It also reckons with the digital forces that could produce a person like Zyzz in the first place, and how his preternatural instincts for navigating a brand-new media ecosystem anticipated an entire generation of masculinity influencers.

Depending on your perspective, Zyzz can be regarded as the original “looksmaxxer”—though the term had yet to be coined—or one of the earliest forefathers of the manosphere as we know it today.

“I really see this as a cautionary tale,” Poster Boy’s director, Selina Miles, tells WIRED. She notes that Shavershian’s meteoric rise and untimely death left a huge impression on Australian millennials, and that his legend continues to reverberate today. “He had his transformation, and his story has really resonated with a lot of people,” she says. “We have to stay curious as to why. Why has he had this impact on men?”

Through a mixture of Zyzz’s archival content and interviews with close friends as well as his older brother, Said Shavershian—a professional bodybuilder to this day—the documentary circles the question of his outsized appeal during a key shift in human communications. At that moment, few imagined YouTube (launched in 2005, when he was 16) or Facebook (first available to him the following year) as a means to notoriety, let alone financial success. Indeed, Zyzz’s earliest videos amount to little more than a kid playing around in his bedroom; later, he and his pals experimented with showing off their abs and biceps at music festivals and nightlife hot spots, hoping for reactions of any kind.

While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion and mutual support for men looking to become the best version of themselves, he also began to feed off those who insulted him, online and off: “U mad?” and “Come at me brah” were two of his recurring catchphrases. He understood sooner than most how controversy drove clicks, and even maintained fake social accounts to amplify the war between himself and the haters. “He made this page on Facebook that was, like, ‘10,000 likes and I'll bash Zyzz,’” Miles says, describing an incident that didn’t make it into the documentary’s final cut. “When the page was doing well, he switched the name of it to be promotion for his protein brand.”

His rhetoric turned homophobic and misogynist, contemptuous of anyone who had not optimized their physical form. A 2010 post on his Facebook page read: “id rather be dead than ‘normal.’”

By then, we learn from the film, Zyzz had more followers on the platform than the prime minister of Australia at the time.

Behind the bravado, however, Zyzz seemed psychologically unprepared for the limelight. In addition to using steroids to sculpt his Renaissance-worthy physique (he and the fitness personalities in his orbit were known as the “Aesthetics Crew”), he took Xanax to deal with the stress and paranoia that came with being mobbed in public, where he was also frequently menaced by young men looking for a fight.

And while acolytes copied his basic workout routines, his own methods grew ever more extreme. In one video, he bragged about obtaining clenbuterol, a prescription drug used to treat asthma in horses, prized by bodybuilders as a supposedly performance-enhancing substance despite the likelihood of dangerous cardiovascular side effects in humans.

Today, manosphere streamers and podcasters can make millions hawking supplements and classes to vulnerable young men looking to take charge of their life in one way or another. Zyzz, Miles says, was “right on the cusp” of that economy, reportedly making about $20,000 in the last three months of his life, which would now be considered a drop in the bucket by major creators. “It makes you realize how much has changed, because you look at how it works today, and it's extraordinary, it's just a gigantic pyramid scheme,” she says.

Poster Boy leaves it up to the viewer to decide the extent to which Zyzz served as a template for the likes of misogynist influencer Andrew Tate, who flashes onscreen in one sequence. (He and his brother, Tristan Tate, are currently fighting extradition from the US to the UK on charges of rape and sex trafficking that their attorney has claimed are without merit.) Setting aside some provocative aspects of behavior, Zyzz did not appear to preach from a place of nihilism or cynicism, and he had a genuine community.

“Aziz did have friends, and I think that male friendship is one of the beautiful themes of this story,” Miles says, referring to the members of the Aesthetics Crew who sat for interviews and remain in touch today. She wonders if they collectively make the case that a currently voguish explanation for radicalization among men, the so-called male loneliness epidemic, “might not be the right term for what we're actually seeing.” In the end, she notes, it was Zyzz who isolated himself from this network as they sought to help him.

Zyzz traveled alone to Thailand in July 2011, having told each of his closest friends that he was traveling with another one of them. After his death, Thai authorities revealed that he purchased a wide variety of pharmaceutical drugs and underwent multiple facial surgeries while in the country. Those who went to identify his body upon its return to Australia recount how they could barely recognize him due to those procedures.

The exact cause of Shavershian’s death was never made public until Poster Boy disclosed the findings of his toxicology report: acute respiratory failure brought on by a combination of morphine, cocaine, and benzodiazepines.

Perhaps it was unavoidable that Zyzz would be mythologized as a martyr for the manosphere. The closing credits of the film show a montage of tattoos in his memory. His brother Said, who runs a fitness brand, sells T-shirts with illustrations of both of their faces and a zeitgeisty, looksmaxxing slogan that would have made little sense 15 years ago: “Mog Them All.” (He continues to follow Zyzz’s playbook when it comes to courting controversy, too, and is shown recording a podcast in which he argues that there is “no such thing as toxic masculinity.”)

But Miles would like viewers to take different lessons from what happened to Shavershian as he evolved into Zyzz, fracturing his real identity in the process of building up the kind of facade that is all too common in the influencer age he prefigured.

“This was this persona that he created, and he felt that it was separate from who he really was, that it was OK to take risks,” Miles says. “It was so successful, and it did kind of take over his life.” Whatever good intentions and ideals he may have had, the incentives of the algorithm “corrupted those, and changed him as a person,” she says.

Yet his formula has clearly endured. There are still a lot of young men who want to hear “that you can be the master of your own universe, you can have some control over your fate, and you can be who you wanna be,” Miles says. “More than ever, men are seeking that sense of hope. And Zyzz kind of gave that to them.”

entries.title: 5 Best Apple Watch Bands: Nike, Nomad, and Hermés (2026)
entries.summary: We’ve been testing bands since the first Apple Watch launched in 2015. From silicone sports straps to leather bands, I’ve rounded up the best for every occasion.
entries.content:
Apple Watches are smart little gadgets, but they don't always fit the vibe. There were plenty of nights when I left mine at home because, as much as I wanted to check my notifications discreetly, the watch just didn't match my outfit. I've also had my fair share of faux pas and just let the neon orange sport band clash with my neutral ensemble.

Fortunately, Apple Watch bands are a simple and relatively affordable way to zhuzh up the look of your wearable. Beyond aesthetics, different styles also impact performance and functionality. For example, I don't want a heavy stainless steel or high-quality leather band weighing me down during a sweaty workout, just as I wouldn't wear a flimsy silicone band to a dinner party.

At WIRED, we've been testing bands since the very first Apple Watch launched in 2015. After years of wearing and swapping, I've rounded up the best bands for every occasion. Be sure to check out our related product guides, including the Best Apple Watch Accessories, Best Apple Watch, and Best Smartwatches for more recommendations.

Featured in This Guide

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Updated August 2026: I added a comparison chart, along with the Apple Sport Band to Honorable Mentions. Prices and links were also updated.

How I Test Apple Watch Bands

I research Apple Watch bands across major retailers, including Apple, Amazon, and Nike. I also consulted former WIRED editor Adrienne So, who had covered fitness trackers and Apple Watch bands for a decade. I look for bestsellers, affordable dupes, and niche finds.

I test Apple Watch bands all day, every day, across workouts, commutes, and overnight. Each band is worn for at least two weeks and subjected to sweat, water, and everyday friction. That's typically enough time to evaluate comfort, quality, and durability. If it's severely uncomfortable or triggers skin irritation on the first day of testing, it is ruled out. My top picks remain in my rotation for months so I can compare them against newer models and assess how they hold up over time.

  • Comfort: Apple Watch bands shouldn't pinch, trap moisture, or feel insecure. I also pay attention to breathability and potential irritation, especially with silicone and metal bands, and factor in how different skin types might react over time.
  • Quality: Closures are fastened, unfastened, and adjusted repeatedly to see how they hold up. A good band should lock in place, adjust easily with one hand, and resist loosening over time. I also examine materials for flexibility, finish, and overall craftsmanship.
  • Durability: To test claims of water resistance, I wear each band while I wash my hands, trek through the Chicago rain, and shower (if the brand says it's safe). Whenever relevant, I revisit bands after extended wear. I track discoloration, odor retention, and hardware fatigue.
  • Ease of setup and use: I swap bands across multiple Apple Watch case sizes to ensure the lugs slide in easily and lock securely. I also judge how easy they are to install and remove.
  • Adjustability and sizing: I test fit across a range of wrist sizes—with help from former WIRED editors Adrienne So and Martin Cizmar—and note whether the brands offer inclusive sizing.
  • Versatility: I wear each band in casual, work, and dressier settings to see how well it adapts to different environments. I also note whether it complements different finishes and case colors.

Most of the Apple Watch bands remain in storage so I can continue long-term testing and compare newer releases against older models. Any discontinued models are donated once testing is complete.

What Am I Testing Next?

I'm testing the Nomad Sport Band. I'm also reevaluating the Nomad Tempo Band, the Apple Trail Loop, and the Apple Milanese Titanium Band.

Best Band for Everyday Wear

The Nike Sport Loop has been my everyday band since 2020. I bought another in 2023 because I wanted to swap colors, and I figured after three years, I should buy a brand-new one, but it has held up remarkably well. Made from a blend of recycled polyester, spandex, and nylon, it's breathable and lightweight. The double-layered nylon weave is designed with dense loops that help prevent moisture from getting trapped against your skin. As long as you regularly hand-wash it to rid it of sweat buildup and dirt, it stays odor-free.

The hook-and-loop fastener and pull tab make it easy to adjust with one hand. It is Velcro, so beware—it can snag on softer fabrics. Still, for a band designed with sports in mind, it's understated enough to wear almost anywhere. I wouldn't wear it to a formal event, but for the office or casual social events, it's perfect.

Specs
Materials Recycled polyester, recycled spandex, recycled nylon
Colors 5 (midnight black, alpenglow pink, blue ribbon, veiled grey, volt splash)
Compatibility 38, 40, 41 mm; 38, 40, 41, 42 mm; 44, 45, 46, 49 mm

Best Titanium Apple Watch Band

Nomad originally designed the Stratos Band for the Apple Watch Ultra, but it fits just as well with the SE and Series 1 through 11. It's easy to adjust, refined enough for the office, and backed by Grade 4 titanium hardware with a scratch-resistant DLC coating. FKM rubber links (PFA-free and antimicrobial, according to Nomad) add flexibility, durability, and water resistance. The clasp is made with corrosion-resistant N52 magnets, which make it effortless to snap on, and it's designed with a manual release button, so you don't have to worry about it accidentally falling off. It's technically suited for workouts and outdoor use, but it is a hefty band that I personally prefer for casual everyday wear.

The hardware comes in natural or black finishes, which is nice if you're particular about matching your setup. The FKM rubber comes in four different colorways, including a limited-edition icy blue that glows in the dark. The glow effect is short-lived (roughly 10 to 20 minutes), and based on online feedback, more of a novelty than a standout feature.

Specs
Materials Grade 4 titanium, FKM
Colors 4 (black, ultra orange, volt, icy blue glow)
Compatibility 44, 45, 46, 49 mm

Best Silicone Apple Watch Band

Moft's Snap Duo Watch Band is made from nontoxic, food-grade silicone, but you wouldn't know it at a glance. The pebbled finish mimics leather, giving it a more elevated look, without the stiffness or upkeep. Also, unlike leather, it's noticeably soft, waterproof, and resistant to direct, which makes it just as suitable for workouts and water sports as it is for the office.

The design is particularly interesting. Each band features two colors, and thanks to a bidirectional connector, you can flip and swap sides to create four different looks. Switching it up is easy, and the magnetic link is even easier to snap on. Keep in mind, there's no manual release mechanism, so it may not feel sturdy on its own. Moft includes a removable buckle as an extra precaution, and while it takes a bit of fiddling to attach, it's worth using for a more secure fit.

Specs
Materials Silicone, stainless steel
Colors 5 (wake orange/swell blue, strike yellow/poise purple, roam green/beyond blue, vast black/stardust, wade blue/echo gray)
Compatibility 38, 40, 41, 42 mm; 42, 44, 45, 46, 49 mm

Best Leather Apple Watch Band

Former WIRED editor Adrienne So says the Moher Green—inspired by Ireland's Cliffs of Moher—is the most beautiful band she's ever worn. The color is rich, but Konsu NYC also offers seven other colors that are just as vibrant. The top and bottom layers are 100 percent top-grain calfskin leather, and the middle layer is a proprietary, thin fiber that the company claims is 15 times stronger than steel. The hardware is 316-grade stainless steel that is laser etched, machine polished, and PVD coated, which makes it scratch- and corrosion-resistant. You can also customize the adapter and buckle finishes to be either silver, gold, or black.

Specs
Materials Calfskin leather, stainless steel
Colors 8 (Empire black, Menara brown, Taormina tan, Serengeti yellow, Arashiyama white, Retiro red, Moher green, Bariloche blue)
Compatibility 40, 41, 42 mm; 44, 45, 46 mm; 49 mm

Best Designer Apple Watch Band

I purchased the Hermés band last year after the orange Alpine Loop on my Ultra got too sooty to continue into a third year of honorable service. The Hermés band is an equally loud orange, but no one ever asks about it; it's relatively discreet as luxury goods go. Installation is a breeze, and the color comes close to matching the titanium case, with a tad extra silvery shine.

The fluoroelastomer feels soft but sturdy against the skin and washes better than the Alpine Loop. I especially like the brand-stamped quick-release clasp (deployment buckle), which makes it a breeze to take on or off with a quick squeeze on the sides. It runs large, and I would not recommend it to people with small wrists, as I'm a large man and using the third of seven notches. After a year of daily wear, there is a little darkening around the clasp from my dragging my wrists around my desk, but that's the part of the band that the fewest people see. —Martin Cizmar

Specs
Materials Fluoroelastomer
Colors 6 (orange, bleu pastel, jaune, grège, blanc, noir)
Compatibility 44, 45, 46, 49 mm

Nomad Stratos Band Grade 4 titanium, FKM 4 (black, ultra orange, volt, icy blue glow) 44, 45, 46, 49 mm $179
Moft Snap Duo Watch Band Silicone, stainless steel 5 (wake orange/swell blue, strike yellow/poise purple, roam green/beyond blue, vast black/stardust, wade blue/echo gray) 38, 40, 41, 42 mm; 42, 44, 45, 46, 49 mm $40

Apple Hermés Kilim Single Tour Band Fluoroelastomer 6 (orange, bleu pastel, jaune, grège, blanc, noir) 44, 45, 46, 49 mm $349

Honorable Mentions

Apple Sport Band for $49: The Sport Band is decent—I’m wearing it right now—and its sweat-resistant fluoroelastomer makes it a solid choice for workouts and anyone who wants a low-maintenance band they can easily wipe clean. The pin-and-tuck closure doesn’t offer as much adjustability as I’d like. My usual setting feels a little too loose for workouts when I want accurate tracking, but tightening it one notch is uncomfortable. Also, if you’re trying to avoid fluoroelastomer, I’d skip this one for now. Apple has said it’s working to phase out PFAs from its products, but that transition will take time.

Apple Milanese Titanium Band for $199: The Apple Watch Ultra 2 came in a black finish, which was matched by this special black titanium Milanese loop. The standout feature is the parachute-style buckle, which Apple claims was historically used for diving and other underwater activities. (I seem to remember that most water activities use ratchet tie downs and threaded cam buckles for straps, but I will let this slide.) The titanium doesn't irritate my skin, and the band and buckle smooth and easy to adjust. It's carbon-neutral, and it turns your sporty watch into a much dressier watch. —Adrienne So

Apple Trail Loop for $99: Apple has several band varieties for different activities: the Alpine Loop ($99) for outdoor adventures, the Ocean Band ($99) for water sports, and the Trail Loop for endurance runs and hikes.

Nomad Tempo Band for $59: If you must have a fluoroelastomer band, the Tempo bands are PFAS-free. It's slightly too big for my 150-mm wrist, and Nomad hedges its bets with sizing by making each band backward-compatible with two sizes; for example, the smallest size is compatible with both 41- and 42-mm watch sizes. This doesn't quite work if you have the older, smaller-size watch, but it fits my 46-mm Series 10 well. —Adrienne So

Wrangler Ranch Rider Calf Hair Band for $35: This collaboration between Wrangler and accessory company WithIt includes seven bands of all different materials, from a turquoise-and-silver bracelet band to a denim band. I was unexpectedly charmed by the Rodeo Ready, which is made from calf hair that has been bleached and dyed. It can be sized to fit all Apple Watch models, from the older 38-mm versions to the Apple Watch Ultra 3. It is comfortable and tacky—in a good way—especially if you're wearing a bunch of silver bangles and beads and patting a horse. —Adrienne So

Zzdzz Silicone Magnetic Strap for $20: My Instagram feed is bombarded with ads for easy-to-put-on adjustable silicone straps, so I bought this cheap one off Amazon. The colors are vibrant, and it is, indeed, very comfortable and easy to adjust. However, the flip side of that is that it falls off very easily, and I can't vouch for its durability. Also, the little loop that holds the strap down isn't attached to the band at any point, so I lose it constantly. Whatever—it's less than $20. —Adrienne So

Avoid These Apple Watch Bands

Apple Solo Loop for $49: Apple really hawks its precisely sized Solo Loops, which form a single loop around your wrist. But they're expensive, and as an active person, I can't size them correctly. They're always too tight when I'm working out and too loose when I'm not. I prefer an adjustable band. —Adrienne So

Hopo Resin Band for $13: My mom has this gorgeous Machete Apple Watch tortoiseshell resin bracelet band ($80), so I figured I'd do her one better and order the cheap one off Amazon. It's a no-go—the included pin remover is too short, so I can't take links out to make the band smaller. I will just get the Machete band next time. —Adrienne So

entries.title: Puerto Rico Is Rationing Water. It Could’ve Avoided It by Harvesting Rainwater
entries.summary: The island could capture billions of gallons of water a year if it implemented systems to catch it as it falls from the sky.
entries.content:
Puerto Rico is experiencing a historic drought that’s led to water rationing following the driest month on record in July.

Yet one ready-made solution is barely being tapped: the normally copious rainfall. Anywhere from 30 to 169 inches of precipitation falls on the territory annually, but the government doesn't require US citizens in Puerto Rico to install catchment systems to take advantage of the free resource—unlike some other island states. As climate change increases the odds of more intense droughts on the island, that type of decentralized infrastructure may be just what Puerto Ricans need in an emergency.

“One of the best unused reservoirs of water in Puerto Rico are the roofs of the houses,” says Fernando Abruña, a partner at local firm Abruña & Musgrave Architects.

The drought has exacerbated a water crisis that was already in motion due to ruptured water pipes and other decrepit infrastructure. For the past week, Puerto Rico governor Jenniffer González has ordered municipal governments to shut off water two days at a time for people in the northeast to conserve local supplies, leaving 180,000 households with limited access. The problems began well before that, though: Many families have been without consistent water for more than 100 days.

While the drought is a factor, the biggest issue isn’t a lack of water, says environmental lawyer Ruth Santiago, but rather the government’s mismanagement of it.

“Even with the climate crisis and these droughts, we still have abundant water,” says Santiago, who works with the local group Comité Diálogo Ambiental (the Environmental Dialogue Committee). “We could be harvesting rainwater right now,” she says as a storm erupts mid-conversation.

The most resilient harvesting systems rely on gravity, using gutters to divert rainwater from a roof to a canister that connects to indoor pipes like a faucet or showerhead. Bigger systems can help collect water to cool power plants and other industrial uses.

Abruña, who is also a fellow with the American Institute of Architects, estimates the island could gather 30 billion gallons of water a year if just 1 million households used rainwater collection technology. The average resident uses 62 gallons a day, amounting to just over 72 billion gallons of residential water use a year.

The Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority loses about 60 percent of the island’s drinking water before any arrives at customers’ homes due to leaking pipes and failing infrastructure. The ongoing emergency was caused, in part, by a series of ruptures in the 72-inch Superaqueduct water pipe, a main artery that services major cities on the northern coast. Repairing and updating the island’s aging water distribution system is most urgent, Santiago says, but rainwater harvesting is a cost-effective solution that can be quickly implemented.

The practice is not widespread in Puerto Rico, where the government has prioritized centralized grids fed by freshwater, but these systems are popular in other island communities. Roughly 90 percent of homes in the US Virgin Islands have a cistern to collect rainwater, and the territory has building codes that require many new developments to include this infrastructure. (Barbados has similar codes.) In Hawaii, Honolulu County even offers a limited number of free rain barrel installations to residents.

“There is nothing that can help the Caribbean region as quickly and as reliably as rainwater harvesting,” says Farah Nibbs, an assistant professor at the University of Maryland Baltimore County’s Department of Emergency and Disaster Health Systems, noting governments should treat it “as part of the national water supply.”

She also says governments should help cover the costs to avoid putting onerous “economic and financial burdens on households.” Yet in Puerto Rico, the government offers no incentives or financial assistance. That’s left small organizations attempting to meet demand.

Since 2010, local environmental nonprofit Plenitud Puerto Rico has donated and installed 73 rainwater harvesting systems for neighbors in Las Marías, a mountainous municipality on the western side of Puerto Rico. Executive codirector Owen Ingley estimates that the technology costs the group $500 to $2,000 for small, simple units and up to $5,000 for larger, more advanced ones with electric pumps. There are also additional costs to maintain the system, especially if a bad storm damages it, and to monitor water quality.

The team recently installed a unit for a man in his eighties who lives alone and regularly experiences disruptions to his water supply. The system doesn’t provide drinking water, but it helps him meet other household needs such as flushing the toilet or filling his dog’s water bowl. “He’s a really sweet and talkative guy with gray hair and a big smile,” Ingley says.

José Pérez Cordero, an at-large legislator in the Puerto Rico House of Representatives, introduced a resolution in June that would order the Puerto Rican Natural Resources Committee to conduct a feasibility study on rainwater harvesting. That would include looking at how other Caribbean islands have made it work and adopting similar models for Puerto Rico. The proposal has gone nowhere, even as water insecurity mounts.

“We are, right now, in the perfect moment to do it, because we are in the middle of a crisis,” Pérez Cordero says. “Sadly, we always wait for the reaction.”

He points to a 2024 law that mandated all public agencies to implement rainwater collection systems on government buildings. That, too, has gone nowhere: Agencies aren’t following the law, nor is it being enforced. Pérez Cordero’s New Progressive Party is in power, but he says his peers have often lacked the political will to be proactive and prioritize the environment.

Rainwater harvesting won’t solve all of Puerto Rico’s water problems, particularly in urban locations where it’s hard to install them in large apartment complexes. They also aren’t sustainable if the wet season isn’t rainy enough—a prospect that’s likely to increase as burning fossil fuels heats up the planet. But that doesn’t mean they can’t play a role in shoring up a dysfunctional system.

“Facing climate change, every year is going to be harder,” Pérez Cordero says. “Every year, the dry season is going to be longer. Every year, the rainy season is going to be harder too.”

entries.title: Amazon Can Use Your Twitch Content to Train Its AI—Unless You Opt Out
entries.summary: When Twitch announced that streamers could opt out, thousands of users questioned why their content was being used to train AI models in the first place.
entries.content:
Twitch has updated its account settings to let streamers opt out of having their content used to help train the artificial intelligence models of Twitch’s parent company, Amazon.

Although the move has reassured some creators, it remains unclear exactly when the streaming platform began using the posts, streams, and videos of its users to train Amazon’s systems. The revelation is raising new concerns about how big tech companies handle their users’ data.

The opt-out process is simple. From the Twitch website or mobile app, click on your account avatar, select Settings, and then go to the Security and Privacy section in the menu. There, you’ll find the Generative AI Training option, where you can disable the use of your content for that purpose.

In the language next to the toggle, Twitch notes that “disabling this option does not prevent Twitch and Amazon from using your channel’s content for other purposes described in Twitch’s Privacy Notice.” These include AI-powered platform features designed to facilitate streamers’ growth and monetization, such as real-time assistance for sponsorship campaigns, viewer discovery through recommendations, and community safety via tools like AutoMod.

The new setting aims to recognize creators’ right to decide how the content they produce is used. However, its launch has also raised questions about how Twitch and Amazon have used that content up to now.

In a forum dedicated to the topic, more than 16,000 creators expressed opposition to having their content being used by default to train Amazon’s AI systems—a practice that only came to light following the update to the settings.

The backlash arose after a livestream in which Mary Kish, Twitch’s head of community, explained the introduction of the changes. The executive acknowledged that the change would provoke a negative reaction. Mike Minton, Twitch’s head of product, also noted—in what he described as “a candid response”—that keeping the option to use content for AI training enabled by default was necessary, since otherwise “no one would participate” in the process.

Minton pointed out that these mechanisms are not unique to Twitch and considered it likely that other companies developing AI systems are also extracting content from Twitch and other services to use in training their models. “I don’t know for sure,” he said, “but I think it’s quite reasonable to assume that almost any publicly available content is used to train models in one way or another, with or without permission. So I think we also need to acknowledge that there’s a lot here that’s beyond even our direct control.”

These statements raised new questions: Since when has Twitch content been used to train AI models? Is Amazon the only company using this data, or are its business partners also involved? To what extent and in what ways is the authorship of content published by creators respected?

Twitch’s Terms of Service, in effect since March 2024, have stipulated that users grant Twitch and its sublicensees the right to use, reproduce, modify, adapt, distribute, and create derivative works from their content. However, until now, they have not explicitly stated that such materials could be used to train generative AI models.

The Training Data Problem

This case highlights one of the major challenges facing AI system developers: the growing shortage of high-quality data for training models.

Although companies like OpenAI have reached agreements with various publishers (including WIRED’s corporate parent, Condé Nast) to use some of their content for this purpose, available data sources are dwindling as technology advances and the demand for data increases. As a result, various alternatives have emerged that are reigniting the debate over the ethics and transparency of training processes.

For some time now, Meta has been using posts and images that users share on Facebook and Instagram to train its AI models. Recently, it also came to light that the company was using its employees’ activity and screenshots captured by users of its smart glasses for the same purpose. Similar cases have been documented involving Google and YouTube.

Thus, high-quality training data has become another strategic resource—along with chips, memory, and electricity—that the leading developers of artificial intelligence models have found running short as they struggle to sustain the pace of innovation demanded by the market. All signs point to a portion of that demand being met with information generated by users themselves, in exchange for free access to everyday digital services.

This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: Google Workspace Promo Codes: 14% Off for August 2026
entries.summary: Boost your productivity and save with exclusive Google Workspace coupons from WIRED. Get up to 14% off plans for three months, including Starter, Standard, and Plus tiers.
entries.content:
Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.

Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.

Save up to 14% Off These Google Workspace Promo Codes 2026

There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?

Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of if you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access – basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace

Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e. update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and it can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized to Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow up message. No apps or links are needed.
